topic: Why the US-Canada Border Is Stranger Than You Think
hook: Your satellite view of the US-Canada border shows a scar, a strip only six metres wide, cut through forest and mountain.
title: Why the US-Canada Border Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
The US-Canada border is kept visible by a six-metre cleared strip, and it hides places that sound fake but are true: a town you can only reach through Canada, a city where you drive south into Canada, and a piece of Minnesota left behind by a wrong map. Watch to the end for the strangest one.

#geography #borders #facts
comment_prompt: Which border place would you visit first?

scenes.narration: Your satellite view of the US-Canada border shows a scar, a strip only six metres wide, cut through forest and mountain.
scenes.headline: A Scar On Earth

scenes.narration: That scar is the border between the United States and Canada. It is real, and people keep it clear with saws.
scenes.headline: People Keep It Clear

scenes.narration: By the end, you will see a town you can only reach through Canada, and a city where you drive south to enter Canada.
scenes.headline: Drive South To Canada

scenes.narration: You will also see a park where families met when the border was closed, and a piece of America left behind by a wrong map.
scenes.headline: A Wrong Map

scenes.narration: Seven strange facts, and each one is stranger than the last. The final one starts with a mapmaker's mistake.
scenes.headline: Seven Strange Facts

scenes.narration: Let's start with that scar on the map, because somebody has to keep it clean.
scenes.headline: Who Keeps It Clean?

scenes.narration: Fact one: this border has caretakers. They belong to a group whose only job is keeping a line visible.
scenes.headline: Border Caretakers

scenes.narration: It is called the International Boundary Commission, with people from both Canada and the United States, set up under a treaty in 1908.
scenes.headline: Boundary Commission

scenes.narration: They keep a strip about six metres wide cleared along the border, so anyone can see exactly where the line runs.
scenes.headline: Six Metres Wide

scenes.narration: That is about three metres on each side of the line, through thick forest, over mountain ridges and across open farmland.
scenes.headline: Over Mountains

scenes.narration: Crews cut back the trees and brush, and from the air it looks like a straight cut drawn across the wilderness.
scenes.headline: A Straight Cut

scenes.narration: Along the strip stand markers made of stone, metal and concrete, so nobody can say they did not know where the line was.
scenes.headline: Stone Border Markers

scenes.narration: Much of the western border follows the 49th parallel, a line of latitude that mathematicians drew on a globe.
scenes.headline: The 49th Parallel

scenes.narration: Alaska's eastern edge follows a line of longitude instead, the 141st meridian, running north all the way to the Arctic Ocean.
scenes.headline: Alaska's Straight Edge

scenes.narration: So a line drawn on a globe becomes a real strip in a real forest, and the trees keep trying to grow back.
scenes.headline: Trees Grow Back

scenes.narration: And that is the quiet part. Next, a city where you drive south to enter Canada.
scenes.headline: Next: South To Canada

scenes.narration: Fact two: there is a place where you drive south from America to reach Canada, and it is not a mistake.
scenes.headline: South Into Canada

scenes.narration: Stand in Detroit, Michigan, and look across the river. The city you see is Windsor, in Ontario, Canada.
scenes.headline: Detroit Meets Windsor

scenes.narration: Windsor sits south of Detroit. Cross the Ambassador Bridge or take the tunnel, and you head south into another country.
scenes.headline: Windsor Is South

scenes.narration: Most people picture Canada straight up north from America. Here, the map bends the other way and the compass looks wrong.
scenes.headline: The Compass Lies

scenes.narration: The reason is the river. The Detroit River twists around, and the border follows the middle of the water.
scenes.headline: The River Decides

scenes.narration: Many people cross here every day for work, shopping and hockey games, and the trucks never really stop.
scenes.headline: Daily Crossings

scenes.narration: The Ambassador Bridge is one of the busiest crossings between the two countries, carrying car parts and goods all day.
scenes.headline: A Busy Bridge

scenes.narration: So if your GPS says head south to Canada, it is not broken. It is just the map.
scenes.headline: GPS Is Not Broken

scenes.narration: Now, a border does not always have to stop you. Sometimes it can feel like a handshake.
scenes.headline: A Friendly Border

scenes.narration: The next place goes further. There, the border is a park where you can stand in both countries at once.
scenes.headline: A Park On The Line

scenes.narration: Fact three: a park where the border is a line in the grass, and where families met when the border was shut.
scenes.headline: Peace Arch Park

scenes.narration: It is called Peace Arch Park, between Blaine in Washington state and Surrey in British Columbia.
scenes.headline: Blaine And Surrey

scenes.narration: A white arch was built right on the line in 1921, to celebrate the peace between the two countries since the War of 1812.
scenes.headline: The White Arch

scenes.narration: Walk in from either side, wander across the gardens, and you can stand with one foot in each country.
scenes.headline: One Foot Each Side

scenes.narration: There is one rule. You cannot walk on into the other country; you have to leave the way you came.
scenes.headline: One Simple Rule

scenes.narration: In 2020, when the border was closed for COVID, the park stayed open, and it became a place to meet.
scenes.headline: Closed Border, Open Park

scenes.narration: Families split by the closure met on the grass, each person on their own side, for the first time in months.
scenes.headline: Families Reunited

scenes.narration: There is no wall in the middle. Just flowers, a few markers and an arch with a message about peace.
scenes.headline: No Wall Here

scenes.narration: That is a border at its friendliest. Now, a town that is American but has no road to America.
scenes.headline: A Town Cut Off

scenes.narration: Fact four: Hyder, Alaska, a tiny American town at the end of a road that only goes through Canada.
scenes.headline: Hyder, Alaska

scenes.narration: You cannot drive to Hyder from the rest of Alaska. The only road in comes from Stewart, in British Columbia.
scenes.headline: Only Road: Canada

scenes.narration: Drive from Stewart into Hyder, and there is no American checkpoint waiting for you. You simply roll in.
scenes.headline: No Check Going In

scenes.narration: The checkpoint is Canadian, and you meet it when you leave Hyder. The check happens on the way out.
scenes.headline: Checked On Exit

scenes.narration: That is the reverse of what you expect: the country you are leaving is the one that stops you.
scenes.headline: Everything Reversed

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places like this, subscribe, because there is a new map that sounds fake but is true every day.
scenes.headline: Subscribe For More

scenes.narration: Hyder is the kind of place where the map says one thing and the only road says another.
scenes.headline: Map Versus Road

scenes.narration: The town leans on Stewart, the Canadian town next door, for supplies and services, even though it flies an American flag.
scenes.headline: Leaning On Canada

scenes.narration: Stay with me, because the next place has a river, three jurisdictions, and people who were here first.
scenes.headline: Next: Three Borders

scenes.narration: Fact five: a community that lived here long before any border, and a line that now runs through the middle of it.
scenes.headline: A Border Through Home

scenes.narration: Akwesasne is a Mohawk territory on the St. Lawrence River, where New York, Ontario and Quebec all meet.
scenes.headline: Akwesasne

scenes.narration: The Mohawk people lived here long before either country existed, and they see their home as one place, not two.
scenes.headline: Home Before Borders

scenes.narration: But on the map the territory is cut up: part in the United States, part in Canada, divided by an international line.
scenes.headline: One Land, Cut Up

scenes.narration: That means ordinary things, like visiting family, can involve crossing a border that nobody in the community asked for.
scenes.headline: Errands Cross Borders

scenes.narration: Mohawk leaders have long argued that people of this land should be able to move across it freely.
scenes.headline: Right To Move Freely

scenes.narration: It is a reminder that every line on a map was drawn over a place where people already lived.
scenes.headline: Lines Over Homes

scenes.narration: India knows this feeling too, where lines drawn on maps have split villages and families.
scenes.headline: India Knows This

scenes.narration: The next two places exist because of the shape of the map. And the last one exists because of a mistake.
scenes.headline: A Map Mistake Next

scenes.narration: Fact six: Point Roberts, Washington, an American town on a tiny hook of land cut off from America.
scenes.headline: Point Roberts

scenes.narration: The border follows the 49th parallel, but that line slices through a peninsula, leaving its tip on the American side.
scenes.headline: A Sliced Peninsula

scenes.narration: So the tip belongs to the United States, but the rest of Washington state is far away by land.
scenes.headline: America's Far Tip

scenes.narration: To drive to the rest of Washington, you leave Point Roberts, cross into Canada, then cross the border again back into America.
scenes.headline: Cross Twice To Get Home

scenes.narration: Two border checks just to drive home. People who live there plan their trips around the lines and the wait times.
scenes.headline: Plan Around The Line

scenes.narration: The cause is a treaty in 1846 that chose the 49th parallel as the border, using a ruler line with no thought for the coastline.
scenes.headline: A Ruler Decided

scenes.narration: The treaty makers drew the line on a map, and the land beneath it simply followed whatever the ruler said.
scenes.headline: Land Obeys The Ruler

scenes.narration: That one line decided who would own the tip of a peninsula, without anyone really noticing at the time.
scenes.headline: Nobody Noticed

scenes.narration: The last place has the same problem, but bigger, and it comes from a map that was simply wrong.
scenes.headline: The Biggest One

scenes.narration: Fact seven: the Northwest Angle, a piece of Minnesota sitting north of the 49th parallel, surrounded by Canada and water.
scenes.headline: Northwest Angle

scenes.narration: It is the northernmost point of the lower forty-eight states, a part of America above the line that should mark its edge.
scenes.headline: Northernmost Point

scenes.narration: By road, you can only reach it through Manitoba in Canada. Otherwise, you cross Lake of the Woods by boat.
scenes.headline: Only Via Canada

scenes.narration: So to drive from Minnesota to this part of Minnesota, you have to pass through another country first.
scenes.headline: Minnesota Through Canada

scenes.narration: How did this happen? In 1783, the people writing the peace treaty used a map, and the map was wrong.
scenes.headline: The Wrong Map

scenes.narration: They believed the Mississippi River started farther north, and they wrote the border to run to that point.
scenes.headline: A River In The Wrong Place

scenes.narration: The river did not start where the map said, so the line got caught in a strange corner of land and water.
scenes.headline: The Line Got Stuck

scenes.narration: Later agreements fixed most of the line, but this small angle of land stayed on the American side.
scenes.headline: Left Behind
scenes.visual_query: Lake of the Woods islands map

scenes.narration: One mistaken map in 1783, and today a piece of America is a Canadian road trip away.
scenes.headline: One Map, One Mistake

scenes.narration: So back to the scar: a six-metre strip in the forest, kept clear so two countries never argue about where the line is.
scenes.headline: Back To The Scar

scenes.narration: Every strange thing we saw today came from lines drawn by hand, on maps that were sometimes wrong.
scenes.headline: Lines Drawn By Hand

scenes.headline: Next: Japan
